overview: At the confluence of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers, Mapungubwe developed within a landscape of successive settlements and regional exchange. Its archaeology connects political change with architecture, farming and trade.

items.text: Gold and ivory linked the interior with East African ports and wider Indian Ocean networks. Imported glass beads and ceramics preserve traces of these connections.
Fertile land near the river confluence supported settlement and food production. The wider landscape matters as much as the royal hill.
Successive centers at Schroda, Leopard's Kopje and Mapungubwe record changes in settlement organization.
The major settlement declined around the end of the thirteenth century. Environmental vulnerability is part of the heritage interpretation, not proof of conquest by a named successor.
